newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawa governor seeks fewer US marines on island.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa governor seeks fewer US marines on island.

text.p: The governor of the southern Japanese island prefecture of Okinawa said on Monday he will press the new Clinton administration to cut the number of U.S. Marines stationed on the island.
"The prefecture will seek cuts not only in bases, but also in force levels," Okinawa governor Masahide Ota said at a news conference in the prefectural capital of Naha.
Ota, referring to the inauguration of U.S. President Bill Clinton and his new security and foreign policy team in January, suggested he would visit Washington early next year to lobby for troop cuts.

The Okinawa governor seized on the rape of a local schoolgirl in September last year by three U.S. servicemen to press Tokyo and Washington to trim the heavy U.S. military presence on the subtropical island 1,600 km (1,000 mi) southwest of Tokyo.
After long negotiations, U.S. and Japanese officials agreed on December 2 to cut back by one-fifth the land now taken up by the U.S. military on Okinawa.

Okinawa hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities and more than half of the 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan. Okinawans have long complained of noise, accidents and crime in areas near the sprawling military facilities.

Facing calls for base reductions on Okinawa and elsewhere in Japan, Japan and the United States have argued that a strong U.S. presence on strategically located Okinawa is necessary to maintain stability in a potentially volatile region.
